notes: Ruling slot 4 = SKJ under Tito (Titoist, but the brief fixes the ruling slot at 4). Slot 19 = League of Communists of Croatia under the Dabčević-Kučar/Tripalo reform leadership (national communism on the eve of the Croatian Spring). Slot 7 = the purged Ranković/UDBA centralist network; slot 6 = Cominformists. Slot 5 = Demaçi's Kosovo underground (radical left with popularity); Praxis moved to 18 as non-aligned democratic socialism. Matica hrvatska in 14 (regional national-cultural conservatism), Ćosić's Serbian national circle in 20. MD slot-22 sprite is the JSO police unit, so the JNA gets no sprite; Karađorđević uses the MD royal-house sprite.

0.name: Pokret srpskih četnika Ravne gore
0.english: Ravna Gora Movement of Serbian Chetniks
0.text:
The Ravna Gora Movement of Serbian Chetniks is the main organization of the Chetnik emigration, founded in the United States after the war and led from California by the wartime vojvoda Momčilo Đujić. Its branches in America, Canada, Australia and Britain keep alive the cult of General Draža Mihailović, executed in 1946, and work closely with the Serbian National Defense and its newspaper Sloboda.

The movement wants communism overthrown, the Karađorđević monarchy restored and the Serbian lands united under a strong, army-backed government. It looks to Washington as its natural ally and denounces Western aid to Tito as a betrayal. Its base is ageing veterans and their families abroad; at home it can count on little beyond quiet sympathy in the villages of central Serbia, Bosnia and northern Dalmatia.

1.name: Hrvatska seljačka stranka
1.text:
The Croatian Peasant Party, founded by the brothers Antun and Stjepan Radić in 1904, was the dominant political force of interwar Croatia. Suppressed by the communists, it survives in exile: since Vladko Maček's death in 1964 it has been led from London by Juraj Krnjević, with branches in Canada, the United States, Argentina and Australia and a seat in the International Peasant Union.

The party stands for a free and democratic Croatia built on peasant smallholdings, cooperatives, Catholic social values and non-violence. It rejects both Ustaša extremism and communist dictatorship and seeks Western support for free elections and Croatian self-determination. Its memory remains strong in the Croatian countryside, where many families still regard the HSS as their true party and the communists as usurpers.

2.name: Srpski liberali
2.text:
The Serbian Liberals are the reform leadership that has run the League of Communists of Serbia since 1968, led by its president Marko Nikezić, a former federal foreign secretary, and its secretary Latinka Perović. They have allies in other republics, above all the Macedonian leader Krste Crvenkovski, who share their impatience with dogma and with party interference in the economy.

They want a modern, open Serbia that renounces any claim to dominate Yugoslavia and competes through productivity rather than nationalism, leaving enterprises to professional managers and the market. They favour close ties with Western Europe, freer media and tolerance of critics. Their base is Belgrade's educated urban middle class and technical intelligentsia; their weakness is that they depend on Tito's goodwill.

3.name: Socijalistička partija Jugoslavije
3.text:
The Socialist Party of Yugoslavia continues the pre-war democratic socialist movement and survives only in exile under Živko Topalović, a veteran of the Second International. Topalović broke with the communists in 1920, joined Draža Mihailović's Ba Congress in 1944 and has since led the party from Western Europe, keeping its ties to the social democratic parties of the West.

The party calls for political democracy, free trade unions and a mixed economy in place of one-party rule, and for a federal Yugoslavia resting on consent. It firmly sides with the Western democracies against Soviet communism. Inside the country it has no organization, but its ideas are echoed by the dissident Milovan Đilas, who argues for democratic socialism and political pluralism in books published abroad.

4.name: Savez komunista Jugoslavije
4.text:
The League of Communists of Yugoslavia is the ruling party, led by Josip Broz Tito since 1937. Renamed from the Communist Party in 1952, it broke with Stalin in 1948 and built its own model of workers' self-management, market socialism and non-alignment. Its chief theorist is Edvard Kardelj, and since 1966 the League has been federalized, giving the republican parties growing weight.

The League keeps its monopoly of power but rejects Soviet tutelage, having condemned the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, while trading with both blocs and leading the Non-Aligned Movement. Its base is the Partisan generation, the army and the managerial class. Its unity rests above all on Tito, now 77, whose succession is the great unanswered question of Yugoslav politics.

5.name: Lëvizja Revolucionare për Bashkimin e Shqiptarëve
5.native_full: Lëvizja Revolucionare për Bashkimin e Shqiptarëve
5.text:
The Revolutionary Movement for Albanian Unity is an underground organization of Kosovo Albanians founded in the early 1960s by the writer Adem Demaçi. The security service broke its network in 1964 and Demaçi is serving a long prison sentence, but its cells survived among students and teachers, and its ideas fed the Albanian demonstrations of November 1968 in Priština and other towns.

The movement demands self-determination for Kosovo and the other Albanian-inhabited lands of Yugoslavia and their union with Albania, combined with a revolutionary Marxist-Leninist programme that admires Hoxha's Tirana. It dismisses Titoist self-management as a sham. Its strength lies with the young: Priština's growing faculties and secondary schools are recruiting grounds that the police cannot fully control.

6.name: Ibeovci
6.text:
The Ibeovci are the communists who sided with the Cominform Resolution of 1948 against Tito. Thousands passed through the camp on Goli Otok; others fled abroad, where exiles such as the Montenegrin Partisan veteran Vlado Dapčević keep up their agitation. In 1970 they are scattered survivors under police watch, yet still present among former officers, Montenegrin veterans and old party cadres.

They regard self-management and the market reforms as a return to capitalism and non-alignment as a betrayal of the socialist camp. Their programme is a centralized Marxist-Leninist party, a planned economy and alliance with Moscow and the Warsaw Pact. Their leverage depends on the Soviet Union: since the invasion of Czechoslovakia, Belgrade fears that Moscow could one day use them as a fifth column.

7.name: Rankovićevci
7.text:
The Rankovićevci are the followers of Aleksandar Ranković, Tito's former vice-president and longtime master of the State Security Administration, the UDBA, who was ousted at the Brioni Plenum of July 1966 on charges of bugging Tito himself. Ranković lives in enforced retirement, but his network of former security officers, police chiefs and Serbian cadres, strongest in Kosovo, has been dispersed rather than destroyed.

They stand for a strong federal centre, a powerful political police and an iron hand against nationalists, liberals and Albanian irredentism. They see decentralization and the market as the road to the breakup of Yugoslavia. Their leverage lies in old files, lingering loyalties inside the police and army security, and the fear of many Serbs that the reforms are weakening their position.

8.name: Tarikati Bektashi
8.text:
The Bektashi Order is a Sufi brotherhood with Shia leanings, revering Ali and the Twelve Imams. In Yugoslavia its tekkes survive among the Albanians of western Kosovo and Macedonia, above all in Đakovica. Since Hoxha closed every religious house in Albania in 1967, cutting them off from the order's world headquarters in Tirana, these babas and dervishes are among the last Bektashis able to practise openly in the Balkans.

The Bektashis teach a tolerant, mystical Islam that sets little store by outward ritual and admits women to worship. They are loyal to the state and wary of Sunni orthodoxy and of nationalism alike. Their influence is small but real: the tekkes are respected in Albanian village society and act as discreet mediators between families and communities.

9.name: Nedžefski krug
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small network of Shia students from Iraq and Lebanon enrolled at the universities of Belgrade, Zagreb and Sarajevo under Yugoslavia's scholarships for the non-aligned world. Its members meet for prayer and study in private flats, read the works of the Najaf scholar Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr and keep in touch with the clandestine Islamic Dawa movement in Iraq.

They reject Ba'athist and communist secularism alike and dream of an Islamic order guided by the senior clergy of Najaf. In Yugoslavia they seek a hearing among curious Bosnian Muslim students and denounce the official Islamic Community as a servant of the state. Their numbers are tiny and the security service watches them, but they link Yugoslavia to the revolutionary ferment of the Shia world.

10.name: Islamska vjerska zajednica
10.text:
The Islamic Religious Community is the officially recognized body of Yugoslavia's Muslims, headed from Sarajevo by the Reis-ul-ulema Sulejman Kemura since 1957. It runs the mosques, the Gazi Husrev-beg madrasa and the few surviving pious endowments, and in recent years it has gained room to publish, build mosques and send students to al-Azhar and other Arab universities.

The Community is loyal to the socialist state and to Tito's non-aligned diplomacy, which values its links with the Arab world. It preaches a quietist Hanafi orthodoxy, avoids politics and welcomes the party's 1968 recognition of the Muslims of Bosnia as a nation. Its leverage rests on its monopoly of religious life, its imams in every Bosnian, Sandžak, Kosovo and Macedonian town, and Belgrade's need for its goodwill abroad.

11.name: Krug hilafeta
11.text:
The Caliphate Circle is a handful of young Bosnian and Sandžak Muslims who returned from studies in Cairo, Damascus and Amman carrying the ideas of Hizb ut-Tahrir and other pan-Islamist movements. They gather around a few mosques and private study groups in Sarajevo and Novi Pazar, distrusted by the official clergy and known to the police.

They teach that the Muslims of Yugoslavia belong to a single umma that must be reunited under a restored caliphate, and they regard communism and Western liberalism alike as forms of unbelief. They scorn the loyalism of the Islamic Religious Community. Their numbers are minute and no recognized figure leads them, but they find a hearing among pious youths who resent state atheism and the marginal place of religion in public life.

12.name: Mladi muslimani
12.text:
The Young Muslims are an Islamic revivalist movement founded in Sarajevo in 1941 by students inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood. Crushed by the communists in trials in 1946 and 1949, when four members were executed, it survives as an informal network of former prisoners. Its leading mind is the Sarajevo company lawyer Alija Izetbegović, who is drafting a manifesto of Islamic renewal, alongside veterans such as Omer Behmen.

The Young Muslims want a society shaped by Islamic moral principles, a revival of religious education and the political self-assertion of Bosnia's Muslims, rejecting both communism and Western materialism. They look to the Islamic world rather than to either bloc. Their base is the pious urban intelligentsia of Sarajevo, Mostar and Zenica, and their strength lies in discipline and patience.

13.name: Savezno izvršno veće
13.text:
The Federal Executive Council is Yugoslavia's federal government, chaired since May 1969 by the Slovene Mitja Ribičič. Around it stand the federal secretariats, the National Bank and a corps of economists and administrators who manage foreign trade, the dinar and the fund for the underdeveloped south, and who regard themselves as the guardians of the 1965 economic reform.

The technocrats want efficient, professional administration above republican squabbles, a convertible dinar, integration into world markets and credits from both East and West, all within the framework of non-alignment. They distrust ideological campaigns as much as nationalist ones. Their leverage lies in budgets and expertise, although the steady transfer of power to the republics keeps eroding their authority.

14.name: Matica hrvatska
14.text:
Matica hrvatska is Croatia's oldest cultural society, founded in 1842 to promote Croatian language and letters. Since its part in the 1967 Declaration on the Name and Status of the Croatian Literary Language it has become the meeting place of a Croatian national revival, drawing writers, historians and economists such as Vlado Gotovac, Šime Đodan and Franjo Tuđman, and it is opening branches across Croatia.

Matica defends Croatian language, history and culture against what it sees as Belgrade centralism and demands that Croatia keep the foreign currency earned by its tourism and shipping. It professes loyalty to the federation but wants far wider sovereignty for the republics. Its leverage is its growing appeal among students, the intelligentsia and the Catholic middle classes of Zagreb and Dalmatia.

15.name: Crvena buržoazija
15.text:
The Red Bourgeoisie is the name the striking students of June 1968 hurled at Yugoslavia's new economic elite: the general directors of the big enterprises, the Belgrade banks and foreign trade houses such as Genex, and builders like Energoprojekt, which put up dams, ports and hotels across the non-aligned world. Since the 1965 reform, control of credit and export earnings has given them power the party never planned for.

They favour enterprise autonomy, profit, Western licences and loans, and a tame role for the workers' councils, and they resent both egalitarian campaigns and republican protectionism. Their company villas, cars and trips abroad make them unpopular, but their money and connections reach deep into the party and the federal administration.

16.name: Slovenski liberalci
16.text:
The Slovene Liberals are the reformers around Stane Kavčič, president of Slovenia's Executive Council since 1967, who in the 'road affair' of summer 1969 openly protested when the federal government left Slovene motorway sections out of a World Bank loan. They speak for Yugoslavia's richest and most Western republic, its exporters, engineers and economists.

They want a genuine market economy, free movement of capital, room for private initiative and small business, and an opening toward Austria, Italy and the European Economic Community. They see federal redistribution to the south as a drain on Slovene productivity. Their leverage is Slovenia's economic weight; their weakness is that the party veterans around Edvard Kardelj regard their course as a threat to socialism itself.

17.name: Pokret gorana
17.text:
The Goran Movement grew out of the postwar youth tree-planting brigades, whose volunteers, the gorani, reforest bare karst slopes and eroded hillsides across the country. Its local societies, linked to schools, forestry offices and the Youth League, form one of the broadest conservation networks in Yugoslavia, alongside the mountaineering clubs and the republican institutes for nature protection.

The movement promotes afforestation, the protection of forests, lakes and national parks such as Plitvice and Durmitor, and environmental education for the young. It increasingly warns against pollution from new heavy industry, careless dam projects and uncontrolled tourist building on the Adriatic coast. Its leverage is modest but wide, resting on teachers, foresters and youth activists in every republic.

18.name: Praxis
18.text:
The Praxis Group is a circle of Marxist philosophers and sociologists at the universities of Zagreb and Belgrade who have published the journal Praxis since 1964 and run the Korčula Summer School, attended by Herbert Marcuse, Ernst Bloch and Jürgen Habermas. Its leading figures include Gajo Petrović, Milan Kangrga, Rudi Supek, Mihailo Marković and Ljubomir Tadić, and its teaching inspired the student revolt of June 1968.

Praxis calls for a humanist socialism in which self-management is real rather than a facade, with free criticism, an end to bureaucratic privilege and genuine workers' democracy. It condemns Soviet tanks and Western capitalism alike. Its leverage is moral and intellectual: students and the young intelligentsia listen to it, which is precisely why the party leadership distrusts it.

19.name: Savez komunista Hrvatske
19.text:
The League of Communists of Croatia is the Croatian branch of the ruling party, led since 1969 by its president Savka Dabčević-Kučar, the executive secretary Pero Pirker and Miko Tripalo, Croatia's voice in the federal party leadership. This reform leadership is preparing to confront the unitarists in its own ranks and is beginning to win a popularity no Croatian communist has enjoyed before.

The Croatian reformers stand for a confederal Yugoslavia in which the republics control their own revenues, foreign currency and banks, for market socialism and for the free expression of Croatian national identity. They remain Titoists and supporters of non-alignment, but they openly attack Belgrade-centred bureaucracy. Their strength is mass support in Croatia; their danger is being branded nationalists.

20.name: Ćosićev krug
20.text:
The Ćosić Circle gathers Serbian intellectuals around the novelist Dobrica Ćosić, a Partisan veteran once close to Tito, who broke with the Serbian Central Committee in 1968 after warning that Albanian nationalism in Kosovo and the drift toward confederation endangered the Serbs. Ćosić now heads the venerable Serbian Literary Cooperative, and his friends include historians, philosophers and writers of Belgrade's academic world.

The circle holds that the Serbs, scattered across several republics, lose most from decentralization, and it denounces what it calls anti-Serbian policies in Kosovo, Bosnia and Croatia. It speaks for the nation against the party bureaucracy and against Croatian and Albanian nationalism, without breaking openly with socialism. Its leverage is the prestige of its writers and a growing national resentment in Serbia.

21.name: Hrvatski oslobodilački pokret
21.text:
The Croatian Liberation Movement is the émigré successor of the Ustaša regime, founded by Ante Pavelić in Buenos Aires in 1956 and led since his death in 1959 by Stjepan Hefer, a former official of the wartime Independent State of Croatia. Beside it stand harder groups: the Croatian National Resistance, whose leader Vjekoslav Luburić was murdered in Spain in April 1969, and the Croatian Revolutionary Brotherhood, which preaches armed struggle.

The movement demands the destruction of Yugoslavia and an independent Croatian state within its wartime borders, Bosnia-Herzegovina included, under authoritarian nationalist rule. It courts the West as an anti-communist force. Its base lies in the diaspora of Argentina, Australia, West Germany and Sweden; at home it has almost no organization, only the fear it inspires.

22.name: Jugoslovenska narodna armija
22.text:
The Yugoslav People's Army grew out of Tito's Partisan forces and is one of the largest armies in Europe. It is led by the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, General Nikola Ljubičić, and its senior officers are Partisan veterans, a disproportionate number of them Serbs and Montenegrins. The 1969 Law on National Defence has added a Territorial Defence run by the republics alongside the federal army.

The army sees itself as the guardian of Tito, socialism and Yugoslav unity, the one truly all-Yugoslav institution left. It buys Soviet and Western arms alike and plans to resist invasion from either bloc. Its officers distrust nationalism and republican autonomy, and should Tito's succession falter, their leverage would be decisive.

23.name: Dinastija Karađorđević
23.text:
The House of Karađorđević ruled Serbia and then Yugoslavia until the monarchy was abolished in November 1945. Its head is King Peter II, who fled the German invasion in 1941 as a youth and now lives in the United States in poor health. His son, Crown Prince Alexander, born in London in 1945, has grown up in exile and serves as an officer in the British Army.

The dynasty stands for a restored constitutional monarchy as the symbol of a common South Slav state, as under King Alexander, and for close ties with the West. Royalist feeling survives among the Chetnik emigration and older Serbs at home. Its leverage is legitimacy: in a crisis, the crown remains the only alternative symbol of Yugoslav unity that predates communism.
